sourceIssues.locator: Remark after Proposition 1, published p.968; author p.17; published Annals 184 (2016), 949–990, DOI 10.4007/annals.2016.184.3.8, compared with the 29 July 2016 author preprint.
sourceIssues.correction: No bound ℓ_A ≪ log ε_D holds uniformly. ℓ_A can be about √D while log ε_D is about log D. Eichler's argument bounds the word length of the geometric code of the closed geodesic, which is a different quantity from ℓ_A.
sourceIssues.reason: For odd a≥3 with D=a²+4 squarefree, u=(a+√D)/2 is a norm −1 unit and w=u+1 is reduced, with wZ+Z=O_K representing the principal narrow class. Its primitive minus cycle is (a+2,2,…,2), with a−1 twos, so ℓ_I=a. With N(n)=[[n,−1],[1,0]], N(a+2)N(2)^(a−1)=[[a²+a+1,−a²],[a,1−a]], of determinant one and trace a²+2. Its expanding eigenvalue, also the product of the reduced complete quotients in (6.3), is ε_D=(a²+2+a√D)/2=u². Thus ℓ_I/log ε_D=a/(2 asinh(a/2))→∞. Friedlander–Iwaniec, Square-free values of quadratic polynomials (2010), Theorem 2.1 with their D=4, proves a positive density of squarefree a²+4; all such a are odd. This supplies infinitely many fundamental discriminants, not merely a finite numerical pattern. Exact computations for a=5,7,13,21,51,101,201,401,1001 verify squarefreeness, the cycle and product. The remark is unused in the subsequent proof.
sourceIssues.known: Partly known: Humphries–Nordentoft, arXiv:2211.05890v2 (28 August 2025), Remark 3.22 p.20, identifies the misuse of geometric-code bounds for the arithmetic code. sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 2, (6.6), and its proof, published pp.968–969; author p.17; published Annals 184 (2016), 949–990, DOI 10.4007/annals.2016.184.3.8, compared with the 29 July 2016 author preprint.
sourceIssues.correction: Use the unit vector u=φ/‖φ‖ in (6.6), obtaining Weyl(u,χ)≪_ε(1+r)^C|D|^(13/28+ε). Equivalently retain the factor cosh²(πr/4) in the bound for Weyl(φ/‖φ‖²,χ) and use c(φ)=‖φ‖⟨f,u⟩ in the spectral sum. The norm identity and any polynomial bound for L(1,ad φ) give the required cancellation.
sourceIssues.reason: The a(1)=1 normalization in (5.7) fixes φ as a Hecke-normalized vector, while Theorem 4 fixes F to have L² norm one. Duke 1988 Theorem 5 bounds its half-integral-weight coefficient by a polynomial in r times cosh(πr/4)|d|^(−2/7+ε), because its spectral parameter is r/2. The product in (5.16) therefore carries cosh²(πr/4), which cannot be dropped from that deduction. The level-one norm identity is ‖φ‖²=2L(1,ad φ)/cosh(πr) with the paper’s leading Fourier factor 2, as follows also from Humphries–Nordentoft (4.2),(4.5). Multiplying the bound by ‖φ‖ to obtain Weyl(u,χ) cancels the exponential growth, since cosh²(πr/4)/sqrt(cosh(πr)) is bounded. In the original spectral coordinates integration by parts gives |c(φ)|≤‖φ‖(1/4+r²)^(−N)‖Δ^Nf‖₂, so merely saying c(φ) decays polynomially loses useful information. The unit-vector expansion supplies polynomially decaying coefficients and proves the needed equidistribution estimate. This identifies an insufficient stated justification without claiming to disprove (6.6) independently.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix A, published pp.983–985; author pp.29–30; the candidate is extraction E11.
sourceIssues.correction: No additional mathematical correction is needed beyond E9–E10. Read the explicitly displayed expansions (A.2)–(A.3) as t^s times convergent power series. A useful explanatory addition is c₁=0 and c_n=−c_(n−2)/(n(n+2s−1)).
sourceIssues.reason: The extraction objects that the ODE is singular at zero and a nonintegral t^s is not an ordinary Taylor series. Those cautions are valid in isolation, but the paper explicitly supplies expansions in powers t^(s+n) and compares the coefficients of t^s,t^(s+1),t^(s+2). Substitution into the displayed ODE gives n(n+2s−1)c_n+c_(n−2)=0. Its coefficients are nonzero for n≥1 and Re(s)>0, including s=1/2, so the leading coefficient determines the analytic factor. The boundary and differentiation steps are justified by the displayed Whittaker series and integrable majorant sin(θ)^(Re(s)−1). The alleged failure of an ordinary regular-point uniqueness argument is not an argument that the paper actually uses.
